title: Deploying the agent (web app or API)
notes: Deploying means wrapping Scout in an API endpoint, such as POST /chat, so a website or app can send a message and get a reply.
The API key stays on the server, in an environment variable; never in a browser, an app or your code.
Each chat sends a session id, so the server can keep that customer's conversation separate from everyone else's.

slides.title: Deploying the agent (web app or API)
slides.sub: From a script on your laptop to an endpoint any app can call
sentences: Right now Scout lives in your terminal, and only you can talk to it.
In this lesson you will see how to put Scout behind a web API, so Orbit's website, app or help desk can all use it.
You will also learn where the API key must live, and how the server keeps each customer's chat apart.

slides.title: What changes when Scout goes live

cards.title: Many customers at once
flow: Each chat has a session id

cards.title: Always on
flow: Runs on a server, not a laptop

sentences: Today Scout is a script: only you can use it, and it stops when you close the terminal.
Live, it serves many customers at once, so every chat needs its own id and its own history.
It runs all day on a server, and the host restarts it if it ever crashes.
And every request passes through your guardrails and leaves a log line behind.
The good news is that the agent code barely changes: you wrap it, you do not rewrite it.

slides.title: What an API endpoint is
slides.definition: A web address your program listens on. Other programs send it a request and get a structured reply back.

parts.text: JSON in: session id and message
JSON out: reply, steps and cost

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: A service window: you hand in a slip with your question, and a slip comes back with the answer.

sentences: The usual way to share an agent is an API endpoint.
An endpoint is a web address your program listens on; Scout's is called chat, and it takes POST requests, which carry data in.
Each request carries a little JSON with two fields: a session id and the customer's message.
The response is JSON too: Scout's reply, plus the number of steps and the cost, which are handy for monitoring.
Picture a service window: you hand in a slip with a question, and a slip comes back with the answer.
Whoever stands at the window can be a website, a phone app or another program.

slides.title: One message, end to end

note.text: The browser never sees the API key, the tools or the system prompt. It only sees the reply.

sentences: Follow one message from start to finish.
A customer types into the chat widget on Orbit's website, and the browser sends the message to your API.
Your API, running on a server, finds that customer's session and hands the message to Scout.
Scout runs its loop, with the step and spend limits from your guards file.
It calls tools such as get order and track parcel on the server, and the reply travels back the same way.
Notice what the browser never sees: the API key, the tools or the system prompt.

slides.title: Where the API key lives

left.label: Never here
points: In a chat message or email

right.label: Only here
points: Replaced at once if it leaks

sentences: Now the most important rule of deploying: where the API key lives.
Anything you send to a browser or put in an app can be read by anyone who opens the developer tools or unpacks the app.
A leaked key lets a stranger run up a bill on Orbit's account, with none of your limits in the way.
So the key lives only on the server, as an environment variable, set in the host's secret settings.
The SDK reads it from there, exactly as it has since Module 1, so your code never contains it.
And if a key ever leaks, revoke it in the console straight away and create a new one.

slides.title: The endpoint in a few lines
slides.lead: FastAPI turns a Python function into a web endpoint. Here is the heart of server.py.

rows.out: find or start this customer's chat

aside.label: Run it
aside.text: uvicorn server:app --reload serves it at http://127.0.0.1:8000, with a test page at /docs.

sentences: Here is the heart of the server, using FastAPI, a popular Python web framework.
One line tells FastAPI to call our function for every POST request to chat.
The server keeps a dictionary of conversations, one per session id, and finds or starts this customer's chat.
Then it calls the same run turn function you can try in the terminal, guardrails included.
Finally it returns the reply as JSON, together with the step count and the cost.
To run it, you start uvicorn, a small web server for Python, and it listens on your own machine on port eight thousand.

slides.title: Sessions keep chats apart

note.text: A dictionary in memory is fine to start. It is lost on restart, so production keeps sessions in a database.

sentences: Remember that the model has no memory of its own; your code sends the history every time.
So the server must know which history belongs to which customer, and that is what the session id is for.
The chat widget makes up a random id when a chat starts and sends it with every message.
The server keeps each id's conversation separately, so Owen's chat never shows him anything about Ana's order.
A Python dictionary works on one server, but it is lost on every restart, so real deployments keep sessions in a database.

slides.title: Where to host it

spokes.label: Container service
spokes.sub: build an image, they run it

spokes.label: App platform
spokes.sub: push your code, they host it

note.text: Same start command everywhere: uvicorn server:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

sentences: Where should the server run? Almost anywhere that runs Python.
You can rent a small virtual server and run uvicorn on it yourself.
You can package the project as a container, a sealed box with Python and your code inside, and hand it to a container service.
Or you can use an app platform that takes your code and runs it for you.
Whichever you choose, the API key goes into that host's secret settings, never into a file.
Put HTTPS in front so traffic is encrypted, check who is calling, and add a rate limit so one caller cannot flood Scout.
The start command is the same everywhere: uvicorn, pointed at your server file, without the reload option.

slides.title: Recap: deploying Scout

points.text: Deploying means wrapping Scout in an API endpoint, like POST /chat.
The API key lives only in the server's environment.
A session id keeps each customer's conversation apart.
FastAPI and uvicorn run it; any server or container service can host it.
Before going public: HTTPS, a check on callers and a rate limit.

sentences: Let us sum up.
Deploying means wrapping Scout in an API endpoint that other programs can call.
The API key lives only in the server's environment, never in a browser or an app.
A session id tells the server which conversation each message belongs to.
FastAPI and uvicorn run it, and any virtual server, container service or app platform can host it.
Before going public, add HTTPS, a check on who is calling and a rate limit.

midQuiz.q: What does Scout's POST /chat endpoint receive in each request?
options: The customer's API key and their message
A session id and the customer's message
The full system prompt and the tool list
midQuiz.explain: The caller only sends a session id and the message. The key, the system prompt and the tools all stay on the server.
midQuiz.hint: Think about what the browser is allowed to know.

midQuiz.q: In the flow from browser to API to Scout to tools, where does the Anthropic API key live?
options: In the chat widget, so the browser can call the model
On the server that runs your API
Inside the session id the widget sends
midQuiz.explain: Only the server talks to the model, so only the server needs the key. It reads it from its environment, never from the browser.
midQuiz.hint: Which part of the flow actually calls the model?

endQuiz.q: A teammate wants to call the model straight from the website's JavaScript to skip the server. What is the problem?
options: Browsers cannot send JSON to an API
The API key would be readable by anyone who opens the developer tools
The model answers more slowly when it is called from a browser
endQuiz.explain: Everything sent to a browser can be read. A key in the page lets anyone run up a bill on Orbit's account, with none of your limits in the way.
endQuiz.hint: What can a curious visitor see in their own browser?

endQuiz.q: Owen and Ana chat with Scout at the same time. What keeps Owen's chat apart from Ana's?
options: Each chat has its own session id and its own history on the server
The model remembers which customer is which
uvicorn starts a separate copy of Scout for each customer
endQuiz.explain: The model has no memory of its own. The server stores one conversation per session id and sends only that history with each request.
endQuiz.hint: Where does the conversation history actually live?
